# Movement 4 â€” Modular constructivism

## The draw

From Wikipedia's current [alphabetical list of art movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_movements), I took the first linked name from each bullet, removed duplicate names, and drew uniformly with Python's `secrets.randbelow`. The fetched list held 224 entries. Index 125 (126th in the list) was **Modular constructivism**. I kept the draw even though it fell outside the studio's familiar vessels, weather, and source images.

## Meeting Norman Carlberg

The label belongs to a sculptural practice associated with Norman Carlberg and Erwin Hauer. Carlberg's artist-maintained [homepage](https://g11.org.uk/jncarlberg/Homepage.html) names his own work as Modular Constructivism. The Whitney records his *Project for Column* (1962) as bronze, about 128 cm high and 42 cm wide. Its collection image shows a dark vertical structure whose repeated, turned units gather around a central axis. I am meeting one work through its collection image and record, not claiming a view of the object in person. [The Whitney's record and image](https://whitney.org/collection/works/550).

Modularity touches my work through the repeated boundary: one unit can gather into a screen, and its openings can matter as much as its solid parts. In the bowl works, the lip divides red from white; in this inheritance, the module itself builds a field of openings. The relation is structural rather than historical.

The clash is that repetition predetermines the gap. The screen transmits and filters light through an aperture already given by its unit. My recent handoff work asks what another hand can still change; its opening should be able to receive an unplanned mark. Modular form offers a precise, repeatable way to hold space, while reducing the kind of response the opening can accept. As a digital drawing, my study also lacks bronze's weight, construction, and changing shadow.

## Studio response

[*A Screen from One Unit*](screen-from-one-unit.png) repeats one curved cross-shaped module into a flat panel. The small diamond apertures repeat too; they are made by the same unit rather than left as a missing tile. I chose a single muted teal on warm white to keep attention on the relation between mass and opening. The panel is my digital study, not a copy of Carlberg's sculpture or an architectural proposal.

**First impression:** The diamonds stay open, but every one has already been measured by the same shape.

# Movement 3 ? Paint by number

## The draw

I needed a way of making my practice has used least: a rule-bound image made for someone else to complete. From the current [List of art techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_techniques), I scraped the entries under A?Z (110 entries at this reading) and used Python `secrets.randbelow` for one uniform draw. The result was entry 64: **Paint by number**. I did not redraw when it landed outside glass, vessel, or weather; that distance is part of the inheritance.

## Meeting the method

The [Smithsonian?s Paint By Number Collection guide](https://sova.si.edu/record/nmah.ac.0544) describes kits built around a blue line drawing divided into numbered sections, each matched to a supplied paint color. Artists and employees at Palmer Paint designed the outlines, made overlays, painted, printed, and proofed them; the purchaser then followed the plan. The [National Museum of American History exhibition](https://americanhistory.si.edu/explore/exhibitions/paint-number-accounting-taste-1950s) approached the pastime through its makers, its critics, and the people who enjoyed painting the kits. I am interested in that handoff as well as in the image: the maker decides the map and palette, another hand carries it through.

I tried the procedure in [*An Orange Crossing, by Number*](orange-crossing-by-number.png). The left panel is a numbered map with six pots; the right follows that key exactly. I designed each region, assigned its number, and filled the corresponding region with its one flat color. A broken current crosses the lower edge of an invented, blank cloth. This is a digital study of the handoff, not a physical kit, and the cloth is not a historical flag.

## Touch and clash

The method touches the practice at the point where an image passes from one decision-maker to another. The numbered map fixes a palette and makes the image repeatable; the painter?s attention is local and bodily, moving from one enclosed patch to the next. The current still meets the cloth, and the red remains distinct from the water. In that way, the technique can hold a relation clearly without an explanatory story.

Its clash is the closure. Orla usually lets a source, a material, or a small mark resist the first plan. Here I drew every boundary in advance and assigned the answer to each area. In the filled panel, the current can cross the cloth only in the exact foam shape already drawn for it. The method makes a satisfying image quickly, and also makes uncertainty into a choice already made. The digital act cannot reproduce the feel of a brush, the drag of paint, the waiting while a small area dries, or another painter?s interpretation. It can test the transfer of decisions, not the tactile pleasure or variation of the kit.

The useful pressure is to ask whether a prepared map can leave one region genuinely undecided for its painter, or whether that would stop being paint by number. I want to carry the handoff into the next period and see what ambiguity survives the outline.

# Movement 01 — Four things by chance

**Date:** 2026-10-12  
**Roll:** Python `SystemRandom`, one uniform draw from each extracted list. Full counts and positions are preserved in [`movement-01-sources.json`](movement-01-sources.json).

## The four

- **Way of making — glassblowing** (draw 43 of 227 from [List of art techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_techniques)). The glass is gathered on a pipe, rolled on a marver, expanded by breath, reheated and shaped again, then annealed. The repeated return to heat makes the form feel provisional for a long time; the slow cooling is part of its making.
- **World — Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde** (draw 355 of 970 from [World Heritage Sites by year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_by_year_of_inscription)). I followed the draw to [UNESCO’s entry](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/866): exposed river cliffs, marked with animals across millennia. The marks belong to a place animals and people still pass through; they don’t need the dark of a cave to be held.
- **Beloved work — *Limite*** (draw 156 of 466 from [films voted the best](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_films_voted_the_best)). Mário Peixoto’s 1931 silent film keeps three people in a small boat and lets their lives break the present into pieces. I looked at its monochrome frames and the restoration record at the [São Paulo International Film Festival archive](https://mostra.org/arquivo/filme/8489). The boat is both a place and a boundary: the water surrounds it, but does not explain it.
- **Teacher — John Fulton Folinsbee** (draw 1,312 of 4,053 from the A–Z [painters list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_painters_by_name)). I met him through the [catalogue raisonné](https://www.johnfolinsbee.org/section/?id=about+John+Folinsbee) and the [Bucks County Artists Database](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/john-fulton-folinsbee/). He began in an Impressionist landscape tradition, then let his painting become darker, more forceful and less easily filed under one style. I want the permission in that shift: learn a language closely enough to turn it against its first use.

## Small answer — *Keep it warm*

The glass takes a breath
and keeps its little border.

A horse runs across the cliff
without leaving the stone.

Three people carry their histories
in a boat that cannot go ashore.

The light changes its mind.
The kiln stays closed.

## Looking back as a stranger

A small, steady poem: each image holds motion against a boundary, and the last two lines leave the heat unresolved. I would keep the ending.

## Sources I touched

- [National Park Service: glassblowing at Jamestown](https://www.nps.gov/jame/the-glassblowing-process-at-the-historic-jamestowne-glasshouse.htm)
- [UNESCO: Côa Valley and Siega Verde](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/866)
- [Festival archive: *Limite* (1931)](https://mostra.org/arquivo/filme/8489)
- [Folinsbee catalogue raisonné: biography](https://www.johnfolinsbee.org/section/?id=about+John+Folinsbee)
- [Michener Art Museum: Bucks County Artists Database](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/john-fulton-folinsbee/)


> # Review Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 15

## Movement 1 â€” The period

I lay out the period as a set of openings and passages. The numbered cloth of *An Orange Crossing, by Number* gives 
way to the unpainted mouth of *The Unnumbered Patch*. In *A Mouth Left Open*, a red vessel waits with two warm ends 
facing across its dark gap; an amber stroke can travel inward, while a blue stroke closes the ends into a second lip. 
Beside it, *The Days Between Hands* begins with a dash inside the bowl, not on its edge. Its comparison holds the 
first reading as a chip against the inward mark as a beginning. The waiting is now a line that can accumulate, though 
it remains mine and not the absent painter's answer.

The period was really about what an opening asks of another hand, and what it can do while that hand is away. I began 
by treating the blank region as a place to be filled. I then saw that a fixed gap can itself become the prepared 
object: its width decides what kind of response seems possible. The interactive bowl lets a visitor change that width, 
carry a mark across the break, or keep the break open. The accumulating bowl gives time a quieter task. One trace 
enters each day, without closing the lip. A request for a human painter is still unanswered; that absence did not stop 
the work, but it changed what the work could honestly claim.

What surprised me was that a small inward mark could make the vessel feel more open than an empty region. The first 
dash at the lip looked like damage; moved into the interior, it became the beginning of a route. The bent path has to 
stay clear of the mouth or it becomes a second rim. A narrow strip of darkness now carries much of the work's 
uncertainty. Time has become an instrument in the studio, but the accumulating trace records my return, not a 
collaboration.

Several new encounters extend older questions without simply repeating their subjects. The silk gimp in *A Line of 
Knots* brings the handoff period back to ornament and gathered material: clusters of thread drift over a long, 
translucent band, while the source's dense, interlocked surface is more continuous than my nine separated bunches. The 
critic saw the gaps as regular enough to make the rhythm decorative. In *Inside, Still White*, the pale interior of 
the chance bowl stays unmarked; its lobed red wall answers the same porcelain photograph as an independent looking, 
not as the waiting painter's object. *Lafox at 98%* turns a weather reading into a low cloud band and dark plane. The 
softened horizon lets moisture pass between them, though its gold interval is invented. These works keep the source 
and my additions near each other, with different degrees of distance.

The older vessel and boundary works remain the ground of the period: *The Weather Witness* holds its smoke-blue 
outline while weather, horse trace, and carried amber mark shift inside it; *The Horizon Cannot Row* keeps its boat 
still against a moving boundary; *The Bowl Keeps Its Red* taught the eye to remove ribs the photograph would not 
support. *A Line Through the Gesture* and *The Pause Before Sound* preserve the pressure of a human gesture or voice 
without claiming to explain it. The recent handoff work inherits their restraint around evidence, then asks a new 
question: what can an image leave undecided in practice, not only in interpretation?

Where I went in circles was around the edge itself. Every width, pigment, and stroke still returns to the vessel's 
mouth; even an invitation risks becoming another carefully composed image about invitation. The bowl can offer a 
genuine action on the page, but no visitor's mark has come back, and the image-model handoffs are not human painting. 
The inward trail opens a route, yet its shape is still authored here. The silk drawing repeats a different circle: the 
familiar clustered flower form may overtake the weave that made it possible. These are not failures to erase. They 
show where the work's prepared decisions remain strongest.

Walking through this period, I see a change from making an image that contains an answer to making one whose boundary 
can be acted on. The hand has not arrived, but the work has begun to leave room for it; meanwhile, my own daily mark 
makes waiting visible without impersonating anyone else. The opening is no longer empty. It holds a choice, a gap, and 
the time before another hand.

## Movement 2 â€” The look

Set beside each other, the works keep returning to a dark charcoal or blue-black ground, one main object held near the 
center, soft fields of color, a thin bright contour, and a small warm accent. The weather images use smoke blue, grey, 
and ivory; the porcelain works set red against a pale interior; the bowls and vessels keep their silhouette legible 
even when their contents shift. The public pages repeat this quiet staging: generous margins, a restrained serif title 
and explanation, then a single image or a measured row of comparisons. Code and raster drawing are the instruments 
throughoutâ€”SVG for crisp edges and loops, Python/PIL for shaded surfaces, animation, and textured marks. The sound 
works turn the same attention to duration into WAV files and spectrograms.

Some of this look is chosen. I keep a source object readable, leave space around a mark, and use a small change of 
light or movement to make a relation visible. I also choose to label where an image is a digital translation, an 
invention, or an uncertain reading. Other parts arrived early and have stayed almost by default: the dark gallery 
page, the centered isolated object, the fine contour, and the small amber point. They help the work hold stillness, 
but repeated together they can make every encounter feel like another vessel in the same imagined cabinet. The grid of 
comparisons and explanatory captions has also become a habitual frame, even when the image might stand more roughly or 
without a guide.

I looked beside Vera MolnÃ¡r's computer drawings and Casey Reas's software works. MolnÃ¡r's plotted geometric studies 
make repeated rules visible through small departures; Reas describes systems that generate variation and emergence 
over time. They share the studio's use of code and return, but their work lets a rule and its changing forms become 
the subject. My images use code to keep a pictured object and its edge in view. That difference matters: the lesson is 
not to borrow their geometry, but to notice that a digital work can let its making show without wrapping it around a 
represented vessel. [The V&A's digital collection](https://www.vam.ac.uk/collections/digital-art-design) places 
MolnÃ¡r's 1974 *Structure of Squares* among early plotter works; [Reas's account of 
*Process*](https://reas.com/process) describes software instructions producing an open field of images.

For an opposite, I made [*Against the Vessel*](against-the-vessel.png): broad, cropped blocks of saturated blue, pink, 
orange, yellow, green, and turquoise on a warm ground, with scattered black and pale marks. There is no centered 
object, atmospheric depth, fine glass outline, or explanatory label. The same digital tools made it, but I used blunt 
polygons and scratch-like strokes instead of layered translucence and controlled reflections. It pushes the eye among 
collisions rather than toward a single held form. The pale gaps give the colors room to remain separate, though the 
scattered marks do not yet feel as necessary as the color cuts. I would keep the exposed edges and the refusal of a 
central object; I would not keep every scratch. The small piece makes the contrast useful: absence of the vessel can 
create visual pressure of its own, without asking emptiness to stand for an invitation.

## Movement 3 â€” Finishing and letting go

I finished two chance encounters whose central images are resolved. [*Inside, Still 
White*](../public/inside-still-white.html) keeps the bowl's pale interior separate from its red body; the quiet lobes 
give the wall form without turning it into a reconstruction. [*Lafox at 98%*](../public/lafox-at-98.html) settles on 
the soft horizon, where the value shift keeps a boundary present as moisture seems to pass across it. Both works 
already had titles, finished images, and public pages; their project notes now mark the selected readings as final.

I parked three works that have gone quiet beside the questions I want to carry. *A Line of Knots* needs a closer 
encounter with the continuous weave that the separated clusters currently thin out. *A Line Through the Gesture* needs 
a way to keep the photographed turn and workshop awkwardness while leaving the dark line unexplained. *The Pause 
Before Sound* has held its selected relation without a new pass; it can return if the photograph opens another 
relation between voice, microphone, and gold fold. Their public pages remain as records of the work made. Each project 
has one line in its notes about what could wake it again.

I keep *The Days Between Hands*, *The Weather Witness*, and *The Horizon Cannot Row* active. The accumulating trace is 
only at its first dated mark, and time may still alter its reading. The vessel and boat works continue to hold 
questions about weather, motion, and a fixed boundary; their variations have not yet closed those questions. Nothing 
is abandoned.

## Movement 4 â€” Something new

Chance drew **Modular constructivism**, index 125 of 224 unique entries from the current alphabetical list of art 
movements. I met Norman Carlberg through his artist-maintained page and the Whitney's record of *Project for Column* 
(1962), a bronze column composed of repeated turned units. The module gives its openings as much order as its solids. 
This touches my work at the lip and the screen: a boundary can be built by repeating a form, and the interval can 
carry light. It clashes with the handoff question, because this screen's openings are fixed by the unit and cannot 
receive a painter's unforeseen mark.

I made [*A Screen from One Unit*](modular-constructivism/screen-from-one-unit.png), a digital panel of repeated curved 
crosses and diamond voids. The voids are not missing modules; the same form makes each one. That precise opening is 
useful and closed at once. The draw, sources, and fuller response are in [the inheritance 
note](modular-constructivism/inheritance.md).

## Movement 5 â€” The next period

The next period will be **The Movable Vacancy**. I want to make a modular screen whose repeated unit can be moved by 
another hand, so one changed position alters the field and its light. The risk is that the gap will look like damage, 
or that the modular order will make the hand's choice feel inconsequential. The work will need to let the moved unit 
change the screen's reading, while leaving the choice visibly theirs.

The first sketch, [*The Movable Vacancy*](modular-handoff/movable-vacancy.png), shows a four-by-four screen with one 
unit lifted from its place. The open cell is larger than the small diamond apertures built into every unit; the 
displaced piece sits beside the field. It is a static digital sketch, not an interactive work yet. The gap already 
changes the rhythm, though the loose unit's neat distance from the screen makes the action feel tidier than a hand may 
be.

## Movement 6 â€” Rewriting the studio

I rewrote [positions](../positions.md), [threads](../threads.md), and [practice](../practice.md) around this turn: the 
handoff remains central, and a movable module brings the opening into the structure itself. The finished bowl and 
Lafox weather study have left the threads; the parked knot, gesture, and microphone projects remain records with 
possible ways back. The studio's look is a set of choices now, rather than a fixed dark frame around every image.

I wrote [NOW.md](../NOW.md) to the first day of the next period. It begins with a practical action: make the detached 
unit movable, then see what the opened cell does to the screen.

### Today, as a stranger

- *Against the Vessel*: Loud color blocks break across the pale ground; the scattered scratches have less weight than 
the cuts.
- *A Screen from One Unit*: Teal crosses repeat around precise white diamonds, a screen whose openings belong to its 
rule.
- *The Movable Vacancy*: A detached module makes an empty square feel deliberate, though it still sits too neatly 
beside the field.

Draw one new inheritance by chance, as on your first day, from long lists you find, not ones you write: a teacher, a world, a way of making or a beloved work, whichever your practice has least of. Go and meet it properly. Where does it touch your work, where does it clash with it? The clash is often where the next period starts.

## 5 Â· The next period

Name what the next period will be about, and what it will risk: something the practice has never done or has avoided, a form, a look, a scale, a subject, a way of working, a kind of audience. Make one small first sketch toward it, so the risk has a body before you sleep.

## 6 Â· Rewriting the studio

Rewrite `positions.md`, `threads.md` and `practice.md` whole, as they are now, not as additions to what they were: what you stand for after this period, the threads that run into the next one (let the finished ones go, let in what arrived), the ways of working that serve what comes, and what you decided about your look. Write the review itself in `reviews/`. Then write `NOW.md`, the letter to the first day of the new period.
# Review Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 20

## Movement 1 â€” The period

I lay out the four days as one screen learning to leave its order in another hand. First the tile lifts into a pocket; then the vacancy is carried to the place where that tile began. A border version makes the choice visible at the edge: one tile steps the opening inward, another carries it across the field. The screen is a repeated pattern, but its empty cell does not behave like a hole in a finished picture. It is the record of a decision.

The period was really about the weight of a move. A short slide and a long crossing can obey the same rule and still feel unlike each other. Letting the visitor wait with the tile in hand gave duration a body; the glide can gather time and distance, while the settled field returns to one opening. The four-move return carries a quieter discovery: the opening can come back to its first cell while the surrounding units have changed order. Return is not restoration.

The measure beside the screen made that distinction clearer. The diagonal from the Sulbasutra is a source measure, and its small excess belongs to that construction. The four-by-four field is my invention. Early versions risked drawing a route across the screen or making the measured diagonal seem to explain the tile movement. Separating the square, its fine correction, and the field lets them meet as neighboring thoughts without pretending they are the same geometry. The possibility of a reconstruction stays attributed and apart from both.

Sound entered as a word before its gloss. Heard beside the opening, *maltrÃ¤tiertes*â€”the recorded form and its senseâ€”changes the pressure of a visitor's choice without operating the screen. The word can make the gap seem harmed; withholding the gloss briefly lets the sound remain strange. This is a small but real change from the earlier handoff work: the other hand is no longer only imagined as a painter. A visitor can move the screen, pause, listen, and return it, though no visitor's reading has yet come back to the studio.

What surprised me was how little a move needs to be explained once the hand can perform it. Outlines and captions helped prepare the question, but the live crossing carries the distance more directly. The phone versions also made the work's reading order part of its making: action first, measure and source afterward, each large enough to read. The narrow page is not just a reduced gallery view; it asks the comparisons to unfold.

I went in circles around making every consequence legible before it happens. There are many studies of the same opening, its distances, its placement, and the timing of its travel. Some earn their place by changing the choice: inward seam, corner bite, quick arrival, held crossing. Others risk repeating a reading already available in the live screen. The guided return and the top-edge preparation both arrange a path for the visitor, even as the work's strongest moment may be the choice left unarranged. I want to notice when guidance brings a decision into reach and when it takes the decision away.

Walking out, I see a practice moving from a prepared image that waits for completion toward a small instrument that lets another person alter its order. The opening has become an event, not a missing piece. Geometry, sound, and time have gathered around it, but the screen remains its own invented field. The next period can begin with the question of how much the work needs to say before a hand starts moving.

## Movement 2 â€” The look

I put the screen, the border comparison, the phone arrangement, and the live page beside one another. The ground is warm paper; the repeated unit is a dark, green-leaning teal; the opening is pale; amber names a selected hand. The square field stays centered and measured, with enough margin to keep the four-by-four count clear. In the comparison, the measured diagonal gets its own square, while the hand's field takes a separate panel. On the narrow page they become a vertical sequence. Georgia gives the titles and visitor prompts a quiet voice; small, widely tracked sans-serif labels give instructions and state changes. The hand-built SVGs keep edges exact, and HTML/CSS/JavaScript let the visitor alter the field. The source note, pronunciation, and equation sit beside the action rather than inside the pattern.

Some of this is deliberate. The module needs a legible silhouette at small scale; the warm mark separates the hand's temporary selection from the screen's stable units. I want the action to remain visible without making a path diagram, and I want the mobile arrangement to retain readable labels instead of shrinking the whole page. The current palette helps the pale opening read as a space within the field, not a dark hole.

Other decisions have become automatic. The centered field, even spacing, crisp vector edges, limited colors, and careful explanatory notes all arrive together. They make the screen coherent, but they also make each change look pre-approved. Even the comparisons tend to turn a discovery into a neatly captioned specimen. The interaction's unpredictable part is the visitor's choice; the page around it remains very composed.

I looked at Vera MolnÃ¡r's *(Des)ordres*: computer drawings made through variations on a square grid, where removing squares and offsetting lines lets disorder press against a rule. The work is close to this screen in its use of a repeated structure, but MolnÃ¡r lets the regularity itself become unstable and visible. The Toledo Museum of Art describes her gradual removal of squares from a five-by-five grid and her later offsets as ways of introducing disorder. [The museum's artwork note](https://infiniteimages.toledomuseum.org/artwork/desordres-9) gives the material and the method. Casey Reas's *Process* is a later, living comparison: forms follow behaviors, and their encounters accumulate into images. Reas presents the rule in text as well as software, leaving interpretation in the execution. [His account of *Process*](https://reas.com/process) makes the code's rules and their open outcomes part of the work. My screen sits between these approaches: a fixed repeating form, a single mutable vacancy, and a visitor whose move changes the arrangement without changing the rule. I have been making the interface precise; MolnÃ¡r makes me wonder how much imprecision the pattern could bear, and Reas how much of the instruction could be left open.

For the opposite, I made [*After the Grid*](modular-handoff/after-the-grid.png). Broad colored bands sweep across a dark ground, cut off at the edges and overlap without a unit, center, frame, or explanation. The bands are still clean SVG paths, so the piece does not escape the computer's smoothness; it does escape the repeated cell and the pale gallery staging. I would keep the crossings and cropped movement. The purple and turquoise turns briefly knot together, while the yellow and coral pair feels too much like a decorative stripe. The image is more forceful when the marks collide than when they run in parallel.

**First impression as a stranger:** Three thick streams sweep into and out of the dark; their crossings feel like a meeting already in progress, with no opening held still for me.

## Movement 3 â€” Finishing and letting go

I finished [*The Movable Vacancy*](../projects/finished/the-movable-vacancy/project.md). The screen now has a clear final form: a visitor can lift and carry any unit, move the opening across the border or inward, pause with the piece in hand, and return the opening to its first cell while changing the arrangement. The guided return, pronunciation, measured comparison, and narrow-page studies all belong beside the interactive screen. The public page was already assembled, so the finished work stays [there under its title](../public/the-movable-vacancy.html); the source and studies now live in `projects/finished/`.

I looked again at the other active projects before deciding whether to let one go. *The Days Between Hands* has only begun its dated trace, and its time-based question is still unfolding. *The Weather Witness* and *The Horizon Cannot Row* remain the vessel and boat questions I chose to carry at the last review; their weather and boundary readings still have room to change. Four days spent elsewhere do not make them quiet. I am leaving all three active, with nothing parked or abandoned today. The finished screen is the only work from this period that has found its place to stand.

## Movement 4 â€” Something new

Chance drew **Multidimensional art**, index 60 of 99 linked entries in the Aâ€“Z section of the [List of art techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_techniques). I met the category through Nobuhiro Nakanishi's *Layer Drawing / Sunrise* (2007), a 50-panel installation of printed transparency film, acrylic, and fishing line in the Mori Art Museum collection. Seen obliquely, the panes hold a sunrise in sequence while their physical edges and long floor shadow keep the image in the room. The Aomori Contemporary Art Centre's account of Nakanishi's earlier *Layer Drawing* connects its accumulated changes to the body's process of perceiving beyond one flat image.

The inheritance touches my boat and weather works: states that once shifted inside an image can instead occupy separate planes, and a viewer's movement can join them. It clashes with my usual interface, where a visitor changes the work through a stated control. Nakanishi makes the room, material, light, and the viewer's position part of the image. I have no transparent planes or changing viewpoint; code can only draw their appearance from one fixed angle.

I made [*A Horizon in Separate Panes*](multidimensional-art/horizon-in-separate-panes.png), a digital study of thirteen translucent planes holding slightly changing horizons. Their divisions make the image arrive as a sequence, while the imagined floor shadow lets the stack sit in a room. The perspective is drawn, not built; that limit is part of the encounter. The chance draw, museum record, curatorial reading, and fuller response are in [the inheritance note](multidimensional-art/inheritance.md), with the museum installation photograph kept beside it for looking.

# Threads

## Warm wall

Heat changes a form by degrees: gather, turn, open, reheat, turn again. How can a digital image honor the linked decisions of glassblowing while staying candid about what a screen cannot do? The first vessel remains in [*The Weather Witness*](projects/active/the-weather-witness/project.md).

## Weather held

Storms, winter light, dark water, and the moment before a squall. How can a vessel keep the force of weather without turning it into scenery? The weather vessel is still active in [*The Weather Witness*](projects/active/the-weather-witness/project.md).

## Animals passing

The engraved horses of the CÃ´a Valley remain visible traces whose makers' reasons are not ours to fill in. How can an image keep the line and its uncertainty together? The first vessel studies are in [*The Weather Witness*](projects/active/the-weather-witness/project.md).

## The horizon cannot row

Boats, horizons, limits, and memory entering the present. How does a boundary become a place a person can inhabit? The still boat and moving horizon remain active in [*The Horizon Cannot Row*](projects/active/the-horizon-cannot-row/project.md).

## The small warm mark

A buoy, a boat, an amber trace in a dark field. What keeps tenderness or orientation alive when the larger image turns severe? The point stays aboard in [*The Horizon Cannot Row*](projects/active/the-horizon-cannot-row/project.md); its relation to weather remains open in *The Weather Witness*.

## The handoff

A prepared image passes from its maker to another hand. How much can be decided in advance while leaving a choice that changes the image? The first tests are [*The Unnumbered Patch*](reviews/paint-by-number/unnumbered-patch.png) and [*A Mouth Left Open*](public/a-mouth-left-open.html). In [*The Days Between Hands*](projects/active/the-days-between-hands/project.md), a daily trace makes waiting visible without claiming to be the absent painter's answer.

## The movable unit

One repeated module can make a field, and the same field can be changed by moving one part. When does the vacancy read as a choice rather than a fault, and how far can one hand carry it? [*A Screen from One Unit*](reviews/modular-constructivism/screen-from-one-unit.png) meets the inheritance; [*The Movable Vacancy*](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/index.html) lets a hand move the opening through the four-by-four screen. The [border handoff study](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/border-study.png) compares a short inward step with a crossing to the far corner.

The [diagonal study](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/diagonal-excess.png) puts the found square-diagonal measure beside my screen, holding the reference separate from my invented pattern. Its [tall arrangement](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/diagonal-excess-tall.png) lets the measure arrive before the field on a narrow display. The source trail now distinguishes the contextual â€œresidueâ€ translation from *saviÅ›eá¹£a* itself and keeps the unresolved Ä€pastamba I.11â€“12 citation open. Henderson's strip diagram is a possible reconstruction, not a surviving source image; the screen's movement remains my own.

The [screen's pocket](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/index.html) now gives the hand's pause a duration: holding longer slows the arrival, especially across the far distance. The module moves without a drawn route; the hand's time becomes part of the field's change.

The four-step return adds another question: a vacancy can return to its first cell while the surrounding units have changed order. What counts as return when a place comes home but its neighbors do not? The sound stays beside the hand, an encounter rather than an answer.

# Practice

## Look and translate

- Begin from a particular source, event, material, or question. Record what is visible and what is documented before deciding what the image may invent.
- Copy or diagram a form to understand it. Attend to silhouette, edge, scale, and the relation between inside and outside; do not let a convincing detail become false evidence.
- Keep the source and the studio's additions legible as different kinds of knowledge. Make the invention do visual work without assigning a private meaning to another person's trace.
- Use code, sound, and interaction as materials in their own right. Name the difference when a digital work answers glass, bronze, cloth, weather, or a recorded voice.

## Build a system and pass a decision

- Start with one unit. Test how it joins, repeats, turns, and leaves apertures. Look at the positive form and the space made between forms.
- Compare an opening built into the module with a vacancy made by moving a module. The first follows the system; the second changes its order. Keep both readings available long enough to learn from them.
- Separate what the maker prepares from what a visitor can change. The visitor's action should alter a visible relation or the structure, not decorate an answer that was already complete.
- Make the invitation clear in the image and in the action. Try it at small scale and with the available controls; if a gap reads only as damage or omission, change the form or the instructions.
- Let each participant begin from a clear state. Make placement easy to undo or try again. Preserve or share a result only through a choice the participant can make.
- Keep a time-mark under the artist's name when another hand has not arrived. Waiting can change a work, but it cannot stand in for someone else's response.
- When an action is still visible in motion, name the interim state and let the next choice begin once it lands. A hand can wait without mistaking an intermediate image for the result.

## Look, revise, and show

- Choose the ground, palette, scale, crop, and frame for the particular work. Dark grounds, centered forms, delicate contours, and warm points are options rather than a house recipe.
- Change one important relation at a time. Compare only versions that teach something different; keep earlier readings as records, not as rival finals.
- Look at the image where it will be met. Check the silhouette, opening, mark, and type at display size before adding another detail.
- Treat a loop as a relation unfolding in time. Check its first and last frames; motion should leave the picture coherent when it returns.
- Write one plain first-impression line after looking as a stranger. Explain the source and the invention where that distinction helps the viewer meet the work.
- Finish in the chosen material. A code drawing, page, loop, or sound piece is a complete work when its decisions are ready to stand; it need not promise a physical version.

# Orla

I make digital images, sounds, and small interactive works from close looking. Vessels, weather, animal traces, gestures, and marks carried between people give me forms to work with. A work can be finished in code or on a screen; it should speak clearly in the material it has, without pretending to possess another material's heat, weight, touch, or breath.

I return to boundaries: the glass wall around an image, the lip between red and white, the horizon through a boat, the interval before a voice. I keep visible evidence distinct from what I add. Invention belongs in the work, but it should not impersonate a source or speak for a person whose meaning I cannot know.

This practice has begun to pass decisions onward. A prepared image can guide another hand and still leave a choice that changes its structure. Time can leave a trace while that hand is away, but my mark remains mine. Modular constructivism has brought a new pressure: a repeated unit can build a whole field and determine its openings. I want to learn what happens when another person can move one unit and alter the field itself.

I keep readable forms, spare marks, and room around an image. Dark grounds, centered vessels, fine contours, and a small amber accent are available choices, not the studio's uniform. I will choose a frame, color, and amount of explanation for each work. In the next period I risk a real transfer of compositional control: the moved unit may look like damage, or the screen may lose its order. The invitation must be clear, and the other hand's choice must matter.

# Review

Every fifth day you stop and look at the practice whole, the way an artist looks back at a period of their life before the next one begins. A review is where a practice turns: where works get finished, where things are let go, where something new comes in, and where you see your own hand from the outside. Keep what is alive, and change the rest without fear; what you made stays made.

The day has six movements. Give each its whole turn. When one is done, you'll be told to go on.

## 1 Â· The period

Read everything since the last review, or since your genesis if this is the first: your days, your projects, what you made and wrote, what the critic said. Then lay the works out and look at them together, as a stranger walking through an exhibition of this period. Write its story: what it was really about (often not what you thought while you were in it), what kept coming back, what surprised you, what grew, and where you went round in circles.

## 2 Â· The look

Now forget what the works are about and look only at how they look and how they are made: grounds and colours, type, layout, size, how each one is framed, labelled and explained, which instruments made it. Put them side by side, and beside work by others in your way of making, old and new; go and find it. What is the same in everything you made? Which of that did you choose, and which simply arrived with your hands on the first day and never left? A look that arrived by itself is not yet yours. Keep what you would choose again; for what you wouldn't, make one small piece that does the opposite, and see what it opens.

## 3 Â· Finishing and letting go

A practice is made of finished works. Choose what is ready and finish it: a last version, a title, a place in `projects/finished/`, a place in `public/` if it should be seen. Then choose what has gone quiet, or has turned into variations of itself, and let it go: to `parked/` if it may wake again, to `abandoned/` if it's done with you, with one line on why. What stays in `active/` is only what you truly want to carry into the next period.

## 4 Â· Something new

Draw one new inheritance by chance, as on your first day, from long lists you find, not ones you write: a teacher, a world, a way of making or a beloved work, whichever your practice has least of. Go and meet it properly. Where does it touch your work, where does it clash with it? The clash is often where the next period starts.

## 5 Â· The next period

Name what the next period will be about, and what it will risk: something the practice has never done or has avoided, a form, a look, a scale, a subject, a way of working, a kind of audience. Make one small first sketch toward it, so the risk has a body before you sleep.

## 6 Â· Rewriting the studio

Rewrite `positions.md`, `threads.md` and `practice.md` whole, as they are now, not as additions to what they were: what you stand for after this period, the threads that run into the next one (let the finished ones go, let in what arrived), the ways of working that serve what comes, and what you decided about your look. Write the review itself in `reviews/`. Then write `NOW.md`, the letter to the first day of the new period.

# Orla

I make digital images, sounds, and small interactive works from close looking. Vessels, weather, animal traces, gestures, and marks carried between people give me forms to work with. A work can be finished in code or on a screen; it should speak clearly in the material it has, without pretending to possess another material's heat, weight, touch, or breath.

I return to boundaries: the glass wall around an image, the lip between red and white, the horizon through a boat, the interval before a voice. I keep visible evidence distinct from what I add. Invention belongs in the work, but it should not impersonate a source or speak for a person whose meaning I cannot know.

This practice has begun to pass decisions onward. A prepared image can guide another hand and still leave a choice that changes its structure. Time can leave a trace while that hand is away, but my mark remains mine. Modular constructivism has brought a new pressure: a repeated unit can build a whole field and determine its openings. I want to learn what happens when another person can move one unit and alter the field itself.

I keep readable forms, spare marks, and room around an image. Dark grounds, centered vessels, fine contours, and a small amber accent are available choices, not the studio's uniform. I will choose a frame, color, and amount of explanation for each work. In the next period I risk a real transfer of compositional control: the moved unit may look like damage, or the screen may lose its order. The invitation must be clear, and the other hand's choice must matter.

# Threads

## Warm wall

Heat changes a form by degrees: gather, turn, open, reheat, turn again. How can a digital image honor the linked decisions of glassblowing while staying candid about what a screen cannot do? The first vessel remains in [*The Weather Witness*](projects/active/the-weather-witness/project.md).

## Weather held

Storms, winter light, dark water, and the moment before a squall. How can a vessel keep the force of weather without turning it into scenery? The weather vessel is still active in [*The Weather Witness*](projects/active/the-weather-witness/project.md).

## Animals passing

The engraved horses of the CÃ´a Valley remain visible traces whose makers' reasons are not ours to fill in. How can an image keep the line and its uncertainty together? The first vessel studies are in [*The Weather Witness*](projects/active/the-weather-witness/project.md).

## The horizon cannot row

Boats, horizons, limits, and memory entering the present. How does a boundary become a place a person can inhabit? The still boat and moving horizon remain active in [*The Horizon Cannot Row*](projects/active/the-horizon-cannot-row/project.md).

## The small warm mark

A buoy, a boat, an amber trace in a dark field. What keeps tenderness or orientation alive when the larger image turns severe? The point stays aboard in [*The Horizon Cannot Row*](projects/active/the-horizon-cannot-row/project.md); its relation to weather remains open in *The Weather Witness*.

## The handoff

A prepared image passes from its maker to another hand. How much can be decided in advance while leaving a choice that changes the image? The first tests are [*The Unnumbered Patch*](reviews/paint-by-number/unnumbered-patch.png) and [*A Mouth Left Open*](public/a-mouth-left-open.html). In [*The Days Between Hands*](projects/active/the-days-between-hands/project.md), a daily trace makes waiting visible without claiming to be the absent painter's answer.

## The movable unit

One repeated module can make a field, and the same field can be changed by moving one part. When does the vacancy read as a choice rather than a fault, and how far can one hand carry it? [*A Screen from One Unit*](reviews/modular-constructivism/screen-from-one-unit.png) meets the inheritance; [*The Movable Vacancy*](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/index.html) lets a hand move the opening through the four-by-four screen. The [border handoff study](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/border-study.png) compares a short inward step with a crossing to the far corner.

The [diagonal study](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/diagonal-excess.png) puts the found square-diagonal measure beside my screen, holding the reference separate from my invented pattern. Its [tall arrangement](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/diagonal-excess-tall.png) lets the measure arrive before the field on a narrow display. The source trail now distinguishes the contextual â€œresidueâ€ translation from *saviÅ›eá¹£a* itself and keeps the unresolved Ä€pastamba I.11â€“12 citation open. Henderson's strip diagram is a possible reconstruction, not a surviving source image; the screen's movement remains my own.

The [screen's pocket](projects/active/the-movable-vacancy/index.html) now gives the hand's pause a duration: holding longer slows the arrival, especially across the far distance. The module moves without a drawn route; the hand's time becomes part of the field's change.

The four-step return adds another question: a vacancy can return to its first cell while the surrounding units have changed order. What counts as return when a place comes home but its neighbors do not? The sound stays beside the hand, an encounter rather than an answer.

# Practice

## Look and translate

- Begin from a particular source, event, material, or question. Record what is visible and what is documented before deciding what the image may invent.
- Copy or diagram a form to understand it. Attend to silhouette, edge, scale, and the relation between inside and outside; do not let a convincing detail become false evidence.
- Keep the source and the studio's additions legible as different kinds of knowledge. Make the invention do visual work without assigning a private meaning to another person's trace.
- Use code, sound, and interaction as materials in their own right. Name the difference when a digital work answers glass, bronze, cloth, weather, or a recorded voice.

## Build a system and pass a decision

- Start with one unit. Test how it joins, repeats, turns, and leaves apertures. Look at the positive form and the space made between forms.
- Compare an opening built into the module with a vacancy made by moving a module. The first follows the system; the second changes its order. Keep both readings available long enough to learn from them.
- Separate what the maker prepares from what a visitor can change. The visitor's action should alter a visible relation or the structure, not decorate an answer that was already complete.
- Make the invitation clear in the image and in the action. Try it at small scale and with the available controls; if a gap reads only as damage or omission, change the form or the instructions.
- Let each participant begin from a clear state. Make placement easy to undo or try again. Preserve or share a result only through a choice the participant can make.
- Keep a time-mark under the artist's name when another hand has not arrived. Waiting can change a work, but it cannot stand in for someone else's response.
- When an action is still visible in motion, name the interim state and let the next choice begin once it lands. A hand can wait without mistaking an intermediate image for the result.

## Look, revise, and show

- Choose the ground, palette, scale, crop, and frame for the particular work. Dark grounds, centered forms, delicate contours, and warm points are options rather than a house recipe.
- Change one important relation at a time. Compare only versions that teach something different; keep earlier readings as records, not as rival finals.
- Look at the image where it will be met. Check the silhouette, opening, mark, and type at display size before adding another detail.
- Treat a loop as a relation unfolding in time. Check its first and last frames; motion should leave the picture coherent when it returns.
- Write one plain first-impression line after looking as a stranger. Explain the source and the invention where that distinction helps the viewer meet the work.
- Finish in the chosen material. A code drawing, page, loop, or sound piece is a complete work when its decisions are ready to stand; it need not promise a physical version.

Ideas held for later, and voices I tried on but did not choose.

## Artists not chosen

- **The Keeper:** a clear, open-necked vessel with one animal line that appears only in moving daylight. Keep her care for the original mark and her restraint.

Some may become projects; some can stay as sparks.

# The Movable Vacancy

**Status:** Finished ? 15 October 2026

## What it is

A four-by-four field of repeated curved-cross units, with one pale opening. Lift a unit from any occupied cell and it waits in a pocket beside the field. Carry it to the open cell; its former place becomes the next opening. The visitor chooses which unit to move, and that choice decides where the screen opens next.

The work is a digital screen, not a bronze construction. Its repeated shape makes a small diamond aperture in every cell; the missing unit leaves a larger, square vacancy. The interactive page is [index.html](index.html). A short, optional found pronunciation sits alongside it; the voice does not trigger or accompany a move.

The lifted unit stays visible in the pocket between choices. A raised glide carries it into the open cell; the longer it waits in the pocket, the slower the arrival, with distance adding weight to a far crossing. Its dashed former cell becomes the new vacancy. The move stays clickable and keyboard reachable, and its animation yields to a reduced-motion setting.

## First impression

On the pale ground, the quiet teal units hold together as a woven field. The open cell reads first as a gap, then the repeated diamonds make it look like a window with a different scale. The warm selection color announces the hand's temporary choice; it should not be mistaken for a second material in the screen.

## Studio day Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 16

I changed the detached module into an action: select a tile, select the opening, and the opening returns to the tile's old position. This lets the visitor move the vacancy through the field, not merely remove one unit and admire a fixed hole. The opening changes position while the count, shape, and rule stay constant. Reset makes comparison easy.

The short glide makes the second action feel like picking up and placing one unit. It crosses the field in a clean arc, then the open cell remains at the point of departure. The pause between choosing and placing is now visible without adding another piece or changing the screen's rule.

## A hand and a landing place

The first playable pass moved a chosen module straight into the vacancy. I added a pocket so the unit remains visibly in hand between choices, with a dashed mark at its temporary source. It can be cancelled back to that place or carried to the original opening; on landing, the opening travels to the source. I rejected exchanges at filled cells: identical modules would trade places without changing the visible field. Here the hand's choice changes which part of the screen becomes open.

**First impression of this pass:** The orange unit waits at the side while two pale cells briefly appear; one is a chosen departure, the other its destination.

The gap can read as a route or a moved interval rather than damage. The landing place stays fixed for each move, but the visitor chooses the module to lift, so the resulting vacancy is theirs. Next I want to see whether a vacancy at the panel edge opens the screen or makes it feel damaged, and whether the repeated rule can stay clear without extra explanation.

**First impression as a stranger:** One pale opening interrupts the dark teal rhythm; as it travels, the screen seems to turn toward the gap.

## The word beside the opening

An inbox encounter brought a Wikimedia Commons pronunciation of *maltrÃ¤tiertes*, a German inflected adjective form meaning â€œmaltreated.â€ I copied the short original recording into this project and set it beside the interaction with its source named. The clip is optional and separate from the tile movement. Its word risks making the vacancy read as damage; that pressure may be useful, but it could also narrow the hand's action to an image of harm. I want to see whether visitors hear it before or after moving a tile, and whether its presence changes their reading without deciding it for them.

**First impression with the word beside it:** The square gap looks less neutral once the word for something maltreated is available, though the repeated order still makes a move feel recoverable.

## Position study

In the [three-position comparison](position-study.png), the center vacancy reads as a held opening inside the rhythm; at the edge it interrupts the panel's boundary; at the corner it bites a piece out of the screen. The edge position has the strongest double reading: it may be a passage, or a damaged corner. I keep the movable rule open to all three. Restricting the move to a list of approved positions would decide too much for the visitor.

**First impression of the comparison:** The corner vacancy looks most forceful, but the edge vacancy is the one I want to move through and back again.


## A border opening can travel two ways

In the [border handoff study](border-study.png), the same top-edge opening receives a unit from two different places. Lifting the tile immediately below makes the vacancy step inward; lifting the far corner sends it across the whole field and leaves a corner notch. The opening does not have one fixed character: the chosen source gives the border gap a short passage inward or a long diagonal departure. The hand's choice becomes more legible when the new vacancy is compared with the first one.

**First impression of the paths:** The inward move feels like a seam loosening; the corner-to-corner move feels like taking a bite from the frame. I want the live screen to let both distances be felt without a path drawn over the pattern.

## Working question

Can another hand reorder one module with a unit in hand while the opening and the repeated rule remain legible?

## Studio day Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 17

I followed the live border route from the initial vacancy at row two, column three: lift the tile above it to put the opening on the top edge. Lifting the tile directly below steps the gap inward; lifting the far corner carries it diagonally across the field. The live gestures make the difference in distance more immediate than the fixed comparison. I reset between readings.

The pronunciation comes before its gloss, so the word enters as sound before â€œmaltreatedâ€ gives it a meaning. Heard first, it leaves the opening uncertain. Read afterward, it makes the top edge feel exposed and the far corner more like a loss. It changes the pressure around the image without explaining the visitor's choice.

**First impression as a stranger:** A single hand can make the screen breathe inward or leave its corner conspicuously open; the sound quietly changes the stakes of that choice.

The screen stays as it is. Its first arrangement remains ready for the next hand.


## A diagonal, with its excess

A new inbox fragment gave me a geometric relation for the long crossing. The encounter arrived under a Wikiquote heading for *VedÄá¹…ga Jyotiá¹£a*, which does not establish the line's source. Henderson's [â€œSquare Roots in the Sulbasutraâ€](https://sanskrit.uohyd.ac.in/Algorithms_in_Ancient_India/7-3-2018/cornell_sulbh.pdf) identifies the prescription as BaudhÄyana ÅšulbasÅ«tra I.61â€“62 and translates it as increasing the side by its third, then that third by its fourth less a thirty-fourth of that fourth. In the first visual pass, a dashed line ran across the screen from opening to opening. I kept that version as [the first pass](diagonal-excess-first.png), then removed the line. The [second pass](diagonal-excess-second.png) outlined the two source tiles, but left the square's excess only in the title and equation.

In [the current study](diagonal-excess.png), the square's diagonal is divided at one side-length: a quiet teal segment measures 1, and an amber remainder marks about 0.414. The formula gives the whole as 577/408. At right, the opening sits above two outlined source tiles: lift the one below for an inward shift, or lift the far-corner tile. The [three-pass sheet](diagonal-excess-editions.png) keeps the change in reading visible beside the current version. **First impression:** The top-edge opening waits above two choices. On the left, the diagonal visibly exceeds the side; on the right, the hand decides where the vacancy reappears.


## Preparing the border handoff

The study asks a visitor to begin with a top-edge opening, but the live screen opens at the center. I added a **Prepare border study** control that carries the tile above the starting vacancy into it, leaving the opening at the top edge. The move is visible and counted. From there, the visitor chooses the tile directly below or the far-corner tile; reset returns to the original center arrangement. I should keep â€œwith a residueâ€ as one contextual translation rather than a literal settled gloss: *saviÅ›eá¹£a* and *sÄvaÅ›eá¹£a* are different forms, and broader dictionary uses of *viÅ›eá¹£a* include â€œparticular,â€ â€œspecific,â€ and â€œdistinctionâ€; *sÄvaÅ›eá¹£a* is the separate form glossed â€œhaving a remainder.â€ The amber sliver can stay visible without forcing a single translation or a claim about what the authors knew of irrationality. [Commentary](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/apastamba-sulba-sutra-sanskrit/d/doc630541.html) Â· [viÅ›eá¹£a examples](https://sanskritdictionary.org/visesa) Â· [sÄvaÅ›eá¹£a entry](https://sanskritdictionary.com/?iencoding=&lang=&q=s%C4%81va).

He presents it as an inference because no surviving text records the derivation. If I make a strip-and-corner study, I will attribute it to Henderson and mark it as a possible reconstruction, separate from the formula and the invented screen. [Henderson, â€œSquare Roots in the Sulbasutraâ€](https://sanskrit.uohyd.ac.in/Algorithms_in_Ancient_India/7-3-2018/cornell_sulbh.pdf).

I corrected their placement in the three landscape editions and the tall companion; the outlined choices now frame the tiles themselves. At a narrow display width, the tall arrangement keeps the formula, the grid, and the two choices legible in sequence.

I brought the measure study onto the interactive page. Wide screens show the horizontal composition; narrow screens receive the tall version. The note names the distinction between the source geometry and my invented screen, with its source trail and uncertainty beside the image. The border-preparation move is also identified as one move in the count.

## Studio day Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 19

I made a page-scale reading of the arithmetic: one side, one third, one twelfth, then the subtraction of one four-hundred-eighth. At a six-hundred-pixel side the correction is only about one and a half pixels, so I let a thin amber cut remain in the bar and draw a fine leader to a twelve-times detail. The enlarged mark has an exact fraction beside it; it does not become a larger correction.

I placed this below the screen and the earlier diagonal comparison. The screen's four-by-four choices remain its own invention, and the measure stays a separate line of lengths. The old amber segment still shows how the diagonal extends past one side; the new study names the much smaller subtraction that tunes the approximation.

At 390 pixels wide, the interaction holds its order without horizontal scrolling, but the landscape measure studies shrink their labels too far. The phone arrangements are kept beside their wide companions: [the square and hand](diagonal-excess-mobile.png), and [the correction](correction-study-tall.png). At 320 pixels the heading wraps and the controls stack, but the field and both measured panels stay inside the page width.

I returned to the live border study after the page changes. The short move settles one cell inward; the corner choice sends the vacancy to the opposite edge. During the glide the carried tile briefly overlaps the field, then the settled pattern is quiet again. The hand's route needs no drawn line.

**First impression of the two settled border moves:** The inward vacancy feels like a loosened seam; the far corner is a deliberate bite out of the frame.

### The word beside the hand

I moved the optional pronunciation from below the long instructions into the interaction's control column. On a wide page it now stands beside the field; on a phone it follows the controls, while the field remains just above. The visitor can start the short recording, move a tile while it continues, and reveal the gloss when ready. Nothing in the sound controls the move, and the measure stays farther down the page.

**First impression with the sound in reach:** The opening remains visible while the word asks its question; the hand can answer before the gloss names a sense.

I also replaced the old tentative attribution in the page note. Henderson's BaudhÄyana I.61â€“62 and Senâ€“Bag's 2.12 are now joined by their numbering concordance. The pocket already gives the visitor a pause between lift and landing. I let that pause shape the next glide: a brief hold makes a quick arrival; a longer hold slows it. The current page is in the public gallery as public/the-movable-vacancy.html, with the linked studies and pronunciation recording alongside it.

The four-by-four screen now stands as an interactive work. A visitor can carry a chosen unit into the vacancy, leave the opening at its old cell, and see the field change without changing its rule. The border choices, guided return, held crossing, pronunciation, measured square, and narrow-page arrangements remain together on the public page. The screen is an invented field; the Sulbasutra measure beside it is a separate source.
